items.title: A particle can pass through a wall it cannot climb
items.claim: A 1 MeV electron approaches a 2 MeV potential barrier. Classical intuition says it bounces back — it lacks the energy to climb. Quantum mechanics disagrees and the Sun depends on the disagreement.
items.prompt: What is the probability the electron passes through?

options.text: 0 percent — a hard wall is a hard wall
Around 50 percent — energy is roughly halfway
Tiny but non-zero — the wavefunction decays exponentially inside the barrier but doesn't reach zero, so there's a calculable probability of finding the electron on the far side
100 percent — quantum particles always pass through barriers

items.reveal_title: Quantum tunnelling and a wavefunction that never quite reaches zero
items.reveal:
The Schrödinger equation gives a non-zero solution for the wavefunction INSIDE a classically forbidden region. The amplitude decays exponentially with distance, but it doesn't vanish.

This is why the Sun burns. Proton-proton fusion at solar core temperatures (about 15 million K) is classically forbidden — the Coulomb barrier is far higher than the thermal energy of the protons. Without tunnelling, fusion would not happen, the Sun would not shine, and we wouldn't exist.

It's also how scanning tunnelling microscopes image atoms, how flash memory works, and how alpha decay happens.
items.why: Students picture barriers as walls. In quantum mechanics, a wavefunction is a probability amplitude — and it leaks through anything finite.

items.title: Travel fast enough, come home younger than your twin
items.claim: Twin A blasts off at 0.99c, travels to a star and returns. Twin B stays on Earth. When they meet again, Twin A has aged about 4 years while Twin B has aged 28.
items.prompt: Why isn't this paradoxical? Each twin should see the other moving — symmetry would suggest both should age less, not just one.

options.text: They both age the same — special relativity is wrong here

The twin who turns around is the one who accelerates, breaking the symmetry between the two frames; only that twin's worldline is non-inertial, and proper time on a curved worldline between two events is shorter
The travelling twin's clock is broken from acceleration
Gravity from the spaceship slows the travelling twin's biology

items.reveal:
In special relativity, time elapsed between two events depends on the path through spacetime between them. The straight worldline between two events maximises proper time. Any other path (involving acceleration) gives less proper time.

The Earth-bound twin's worldline is approximately straight (inertial). The travelling twin's worldline turns around — it is two straight segments meeting at an angle in spacetime. The two segments sum to less proper time than the straight path.

This is confirmed by atomic clocks flown on planes. Hafele-Keating in 1971 measured nanosecond-level differences that matched relativity's predictions exactly. GPS satellites have to correct for it constantly.
items.why: The 'paradox' is paradoxical only if you forget that one twin accelerates. The two frames are not equivalent.

items.title: A galaxy can act as a telescope
items.claim: Gravity attracts massive objects. Light has no mass. Yet a foreground galaxy can bend and focus light from a more distant galaxy behind it, producing arcs and multiple images — a gravitational lens.
items.prompt: How can a massless photon be deflected by gravity?

options.text: Photons have a tiny mass that we haven't measured yet
Mass curves spacetime; light follows the shortest path (a geodesic) through the curved geometry, which is not a straight line in flat space
The galaxy's magnetic field deflects the photons
Dust in the galaxy refracts the light like a lens

items.reveal_title: Spacetime is what does the bending
items.reveal:
In general relativity, mass-energy curves spacetime. Light always travels along null geodesics (the spacetime equivalent of straight lines). When spacetime is curved, those geodesics curve too.

The first confirmation was Eddington's 1919 expedition during a solar eclipse: stars near the Sun's edge appeared shifted by about 1.75 arcseconds — exactly Einstein's prediction. That observation made Einstein a global celebrity overnight.

We now use gravitational lensing as a tool: 'Einstein rings' and 'Einstein crosses' show distant galaxies multiplied and magnified by closer mass concentrations. Detecting weak lensing maps dark matter that doesn't emit any light at all.
items.why: Newtonian gravity has no obvious mechanism for affecting light. General relativity reframes gravity not as a force but as the shape of spacetime.

items.title: An electron interferes with itself
items.claim: Fire electrons one at a time at a screen with two slits. With BOTH slits open, the pattern that builds up is the classic interference fringe — even though only one electron is in flight at any moment.
items.prompt: What gets in the way of saying 'each electron goes through one slit or the other'?

options.text: Nothing — each electron does go through one slit

If you measure which slit each electron uses, the interference pattern disappears — the electron behaves as a particle. Without the measurement, the wavefunction passes through both slits and self-interferes
Multiple electrons collide in flight and create the pattern
The fringe pattern is an artefact of the screen, not the electrons

items.reveal:
Before measurement, the electron's wavefunction is a superposition of 'through slit 1' and 'through slit 2' paths. The interference fringes are the result of these amplitudes adding and cancelling at the detector.

Add any apparatus capable of detecting which slit the electron went through — even in principle — and the interference vanishes. The state has become entangled with the detector and no longer interferes with itself.

This is the heart of quantum mechanics. It's not about ignorance. It's not 'we don't know which slit'. It's that, until measured, the electron is in BOTH paths in a coherent superposition that has measurable effects (the fringes).
items.why: Particles have definite positions in classical physics. Quantum particles don't — their position is a probability distribution that depends on what you can in principle know.

items.title: Knowing where it is means not knowing where it's going
items.claim: Take an electron and pin down its position to within a hydrogen atom (10 to the minus 10 m). The uncertainty in its momentum is then at least 1.05 times 10 to the minus 24 kg m/s — giving the electron an undetermined velocity of about 11 million metres per second.
items.prompt: Is this 'just' a limitation of our instruments?

options.text: Yes — better lasers will eventually let us measure both exactly
No — it's a fundamental property of conjugate variables in quantum mechanics, baked into the maths (the operators don't commute) regardless of what apparatus you use
Yes — quantum mechanics is approximate and will be replaced
No — measuring position physically kicks the particle, so the uncertainty is a disturbance effect

items.reveal:
Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: delta x times delta p is at least h-bar over 2. This is NOT a statement about measurement disturbance, despite the famous 'gamma-ray microscope' thought experiment.

It is a mathematical consequence of position and momentum being represented as non-commuting operators. A state with definite position is a superposition of all possible momenta. A state with definite momentum (a plane wave) is spread over all positions. You cannot have both simultaneously — the states with both definite simply do not exist.

This is why electrons in atoms don't fall into the nucleus. Confining them to the nuclear volume would require enormous momentum uncertainty — and hence enormous kinetic energy. The ground-state size of the hydrogen atom is set by the balance.
items.why: Uncertainty is taught as if it were a measurement problem. It's a structural feature of how nature is built.

items.title: Two particles agree faster than light can travel
items.claim: Prepare two entangled photons and send them light-years apart. Measure the polarisation of one. The other's polarisation is instantly determined — apparently faster than light could send a signal between them.
items.prompt: Does this violate special relativity (no information faster than c)?

options.text: Yes — entanglement secretly transmits signals
No — the correlations are perfect but the local result is random; you cannot send information until classical comparison is made
Yes — relativity is wrong
No — entangled particles communicate through a third dimension

items.reveal_title: Bell's theorem ruled out local hidden variables
items.reveal:
Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen in 1935 argued that quantum mechanics must be incomplete: there must be 'hidden variables' that determine outcomes locally, and entanglement just looks spooky because we don't see those variables.

In 1964 John Bell showed any local hidden-variable theory must satisfy a mathematical inequality. Real entangled particles VIOLATE this inequality. Experimental tests (Aspect 1982, and many since, culminating in 'loophole-free' tests by 2015) confirmed quantum mechanics over local realism.

But quantum correlations cannot be used for signalling: Alice's local measurement looks random no matter what Bob does, until they compare classically. The 2022 Nobel Prize honoured Clauser, Aspect and Zeilinger for this work.
items.why: Classical intuitions about pre-existing properties and local causes fail. Quantum systems can be entangled in ways with no classical analogue.

items.title: A bullet stuck in a block loses more energy than people think
items.claim: A 10 g bullet at 500 m/s embeds in a 1 kg block initially at rest. Momentum is conserved. About 99 percent of the original kinetic energy is gone — converted to heat and deformation.
items.prompt: What proportion of the initial kinetic energy is retained as KE of the bullet-and-block system?

options.text: 100 percent — momentum is conserved
50 percent — half is always lost in collisions
About 1 percent — momentum and kinetic energy are separate conservation conditions; only the former is required in inelastic collisions
Energy is lost only if the block is destroyed

items.reveal_title: Momentum is always conserved; kinetic energy is not
items.reveal:
Initial momentum: 0.01 times 500 = 5 kg m/s. After embedding: (1.01) times v = 5, so v is about 4.95 m/s.
Initial KE: 0.5 times 0.01 times 500 squared = 1250 J.
Final KE: 0.5 times 1.01 times 4.95 squared = 12.4 J.

Almost all the kinetic energy has been lost — to heat, sound, deformation. About 1 percent of the bullet's original KE remains as bulk motion of the combined system.

The mass ratio matters: a bullet hitting a much heavier block loses more KE than the same bullet hitting a similar-mass block, because the velocity afterwards is much smaller.
items.why: Conservation of momentum is treated as if it also implied conservation of kinetic energy. It doesn't — only elastic collisions conserve both.

items.title: Classical physics predicts infinite radiation from a campfire
items.claim: In the late 1800s, the Rayleigh-Jeans law for blackbody radiation worked at low frequencies but predicted radiation rising without limit at high frequencies. Every hot object should emit infinite UV. They didn't. Classical physics had broken.
items.prompt: What did Planck do in 1900 to fix it?

options.text: He added a damping term at high frequencies
He proposed energy could only be exchanged in discrete quanta of size E equals hf, suppressing high-frequency modes when hf was much greater than kT
He invented relativity to explain it
He showed the experiments were wrong

items.reveal_title: Quantisation was born to plug a hole
items.reveal:
Classical physics treats blackbody modes (standing electromagnetic waves) as continuous oscillators each carrying kT of energy on average. Count the modes (which scale as f squared) and you get infinite energy at high frequency — the ultraviolet catastrophe.

Planck assumed each mode could only exchange energy in lumps of hf with the cavity walls. At high f, hf becomes much greater than kT, and the probability of even a single quantum being excited goes to zero. The high-frequency divergence is killed.

Planck initially considered this a 'mathematical trick'. Einstein's 1905 photoelectric paper took the quanta seriously as real entities (photons). The entire 20th century of quantum physics started with that fudge.
items.why: The greatest paradigm shifts often start as ad hoc fixes to specific problems. Planck's quanta were dismissed even by Planck — until evidence forced his hand.

items.title: Two metal plates attract through empty space
items.claim: Place two parallel uncharged metal plates a micrometre apart in a vacuum. They attract. The force isn't gravity, isn't electrostatic — it's a measurable consequence of quantum vacuum fluctuations.
items.prompt: What's pulling them together?

options.text: Residual air pressure

The vacuum supports a sea of fluctuating electromagnetic modes; between the plates only certain wavelengths fit, so the radiation pressure inside is less than outside — net force pushes the plates together
Magnetic attraction from Earth's field
Charge accumulated on the plate surfaces

items.reveal_title: The Casimir effect — radiation pressure from nothing
items.reveal:
Even in 'empty' space, quantum field theory predicts a sea of virtual photons. Between two parallel metal plates, only photons with wavelengths fitting an integer number of half-wavelengths in the gap can exist (a quantisation condition like a particle in a box). Outside the plates, ALL wavelengths exist.

This produces an imbalance in vacuum-radiation pressure. The plates feel more 'push' from outside than from inside, and so are pushed together.

The force is tiny: about 1.3 millionths of a newton per square metre at 1 micrometre separation. Lamoreaux measured it in 1997, confirming Casimir's 1948 prediction. The vacuum is not nothing.
items.why: The classical vacuum is empty. The quantum vacuum is full of fluctuating fields that have measurable mechanical consequences.

items.title: The laws of physics don't tell time which way to run
items.claim: Newton's laws, Maxwell's equations and the Schrödinger equation all look the same if you reverse time. So why do we remember the past but not the future, and why does milk mix into coffee but never unmix?
items.prompt: Where does the arrow of time come from?

options.text: Gravity defines a preferred time direction
The second law of thermodynamics — entropy increases with time, statistically — but only because the universe started in an extremely low-entropy state and is far from equilibrium
Time has a built-in direction physicists haven't found yet
We perceive time directionally; physics doesn't have a preferred direction

items.reveal_title: Boltzmann's H-theorem and the low-entropy past
items.reveal:
Microscopic laws are time-reversible. But there are vastly more disordered configurations than ordered ones. Starting from any low-entropy state, the overwhelmingly likely evolution is toward higher entropy.

The question becomes: why did the universe start in such a low-entropy state? The Big Bang and the smoothness of the early universe set up an enormous entropy 'budget' that has been depleting ever since.

We remember the past because forming a memory increases entropy. We can't 'remember' the future because that would correspond to entropy decreasing in the brain.

The 'arrow of time' is an emergent statistical property of an initial condition — not a fundamental law.
items.why: Time feels like it has an obvious direction. Physically, that direction is a cosmological accident, not a fundamental property of time itself.

items.title: There is no centrifugal force
items.claim: Swing a bucket on a string in a circle. People say a 'centrifugal force' pulls the water outward, keeping it in the bucket. Inside the rotating bucket-frame, sure. From a stationary frame, that force doesn't exist.
items.prompt: What's actually keeping the water in the spinning bucket?

options.text: Centrifugal force, an outward pseudo-force
Newton's first law — the water 'wants' to travel in a straight line, and the bucket bottom keeps providing a centripetal force inward that bends its path into a circle
Gravity, which spins with the bucket
Friction with the air

items.reveal_title: Centrifugal force is a frame-dependent fiction
items.reveal:
In an inertial frame (you watching from outside), the only forces on the water are gravity (down) and the normal force from the bucket bottom (toward the centre of the circle). Combined, they cause the water to follow a circular path — the inward acceleration is v squared over r.

The 'centrifugal' force shows up only when you do physics in the rotating frame of the bucket itself. It's a fictitious force, introduced to make Newton's laws appear to work in a non-inertial frame.

The same logic applies to washing machines, planetary rotation, and amusement-park rides. Real forces always point inward (centripetal) — the apparent outward push is an artefact of trying to use Newtonian mechanics in a rotating coordinate system.
items.why: Everyday language ('the centrifugal force pulled me to the wall') conflates two different physical descriptions. Real forces have specific causes; pseudo-forces are mathematical artefacts of non-inertial frames.

items.title: Moving a magnet generates electricity, but so does moving the wire
items.claim: Move a magnet through a coil of wire — current flows. Move the wire through the magnet's field — same current flows. From the wire's frame, there's no changing magnetic field. So why is there an EMF?
items.prompt: What unifies the two cases?

options.text: Coincidence — different physics, same result
Relativity — a magnetic field in one frame appears partly as an electric field in another; the same Maxwell-equation phenomenon looks like two different mechanisms depending on the reference frame
Friction between magnet and wire
Quantum effects in the wire

items.reveal:
The opening paragraph of Einstein's special relativity paper ('On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies', 1905) is exactly this puzzle. Maxwell's equations describe the moving-magnet case as an electric field induced by a changing B-field; they describe the moving-wire case as a magnetic Lorentz force on the wire's free electrons. Two different equations, two different stories — but always the same measurable current.

Einstein argued this was a clue that electric and magnetic fields were not really separate things — they were components of a single object (the electromagnetic field) whose decomposition depended on the observer's frame. Special relativity grew out of this insight.

Learning Maxwell's equations one frame at a time hides the deeper unity.
items.why: Two physical explanations giving identical results is usually a sign that they are aspects of the same underlying thing. Faraday's law was a clue to special relativity decades before Einstein.

items.title: Planes don't fly because of equal transit times
items.claim: Most textbooks say 'air travels faster over the top of a curved wing because it has further to go, so by Bernoulli the pressure is lower, so lift'. The premise is false — there is no rule that the air over the top and bottom must arrive at the same time.
items.prompt: What actually generates lift?

options.text: Bernoulli effect, exactly as the textbook says

The wing deflects a mass of air downward (angle of attack and camber); by Newton's third law, the wing experiences an upward reaction force. Bernoulli is a valid but partial description — the air over the top really is faster, but for circulation/curvature reasons, not equal-transit
Engine thrust alone holds the plane up
A vacuum above the wing

items.reveal_title: Lift is downwash, and circulation explains the pressure difference
items.reveal:
High-speed flow visualisation shows air over the top of a wing arrives at the trailing edge BEFORE air below — equal-transit is wrong. Lift comes from the wing accelerating a column of air downward. By F equals ma, the wing must push air down; the air pushes the wing up.

The Bernoulli formula gives a self-consistent description of the pressure difference between top and bottom, but it doesn't explain WHY the air on top is faster. Modern aerodynamics uses circulation (the Kutta condition at the trailing edge) for that.

A flat plate at angle of attack generates lift just fine — no airfoil curvature required. Stunt planes fly upside down. Equal-transit is a story, not a mechanism.
items.why: Textbook physics often picks one principle and over-applies it. Real-world flight is best explained by momentum exchange, with Bernoulli as a consistency check.

items.title: Light slows down to less than a metre per second in some materials
items.claim: The speed of light in vacuum is 299,792,458 m/s. In ultracold sodium-atom clouds, light has been slowed to 17 m/s — and frozen entirely, stored as a coherent quantum state, and re-emitted.
items.prompt: Doesn't c being a constant of nature forbid this?

options.text: Yes — the experiments are flawed
No — only the speed of light IN VACUUM is invariant; in matter, photons interact with atoms and the effective propagation speed depends on the medium, sometimes drastically
No — but the slowing is only apparent, like an optical illusion
Yes — but only by 1 part in 10 to the 9

items.reveal:
In a transparent medium, light's phase velocity is c over n, where n is the refractive index. In glass n is about 1.5. In materials near an atomic resonance, n can be much greater.

Hau, Harris and collaborators (1999, Harvard) used electromagnetically induced transparency to give a cloud of cold sodium atoms an effective refractive index in the millions, slowing a light pulse to 17 m/s. Later work (2001) stopped the pulse entirely — the photon was 'stored' in the atomic coherence and then released on demand.

Nothing of relativity is violated. The vacuum speed c is the maximum signal velocity for any information through any medium.
items.why: Constants of nature are constants under specified conditions. Outside those conditions (like 'in a vacuum'), measured values can differ vastly.

items.title: A tiny push, repeatedly, can destroy a bridge
items.claim: In November 1940, mild crosswinds of about 19 m/s set the Tacoma Narrows Bridge into a torsional oscillation. Within hours, the deck twisted itself apart and collapsed. The wind force was modest. The destruction wasn't.
items.prompt: Why was a steady wind so devastating?

options.text: The wind was much stronger than reported
Aeroelastic flutter — the bridge's twisting motion modified the air flow in a way that pumped energy back into the same motion at exactly the bridge's natural frequency, amplifying every cycle
Earthquake activity coincided with the wind
Workers loosened bolts the night before

items.reveal_title: Resonance can extract energy from a steady source
items.reveal:
If energy is pumped into an oscillator at exactly its natural frequency, the amplitude grows linearly with time — even tiny forces can produce huge displacements.

The Tacoma Narrows failure wasn't simple wind-driven resonance, but aeroelastic flutter — the deck's torsional motion changed the lift on the deck in a way that drove the next cycle. A small constant wind became a destructive resonant amplifier through this feedback.

Millennium Bridge in London (2000) saw the same thing with pedestrians: walkers' small lateral footfalls synchronised with the deck's natural side-to-side mode, and the bridge wobbled wildly. The crowd unconsciously walked in step to match the resonance.
items.why: Linear thinking ('small force gives small effect') breaks at resonance. Repeated small forces at the right frequency can do unbounded work.

items.title: Atoms weigh less than the sum of their parts
items.claim: A helium-4 nucleus weighs 4.0015 atomic mass units. The two protons and two neutrons it's made of, separately, weigh 4.0319 amu. The difference — 0.0304 amu — has gone somewhere.
items.prompt: Where did the missing mass go?

options.text: It's a rounding error
Converted to binding energy via E equals mc squared — about 28 MeV released when nucleons assembled into the nucleus, which is exactly the energy needed to take it back apart
It's stored as kinetic energy in the nucleus
It was emitted as neutrinos

items.reveal:
The mass defect for helium-4: 0.0304 amu times 931.5 MeV per amu, giving 28.3 MeV — the binding energy of the helium nucleus.

This is why nuclear processes release a million times more energy per reaction than chemical ones. Chemical bonds involve electron rearrangements of a few eV each. Nuclear bonds involve nucleons and are millions of times stronger.

For heavy nuclei (uranium) splitting into medium ones, the products are MORE tightly bound than the reactant. Mass is released as fission energy — about 200 MeV per uranium nucleus. The whole atomic age sits on this seemingly small mass discrepancy.
items.why: Mass conservation feels like a universal law from chemistry. At the nuclear scale, mass and energy are different forms of the same thing.

items.title: You cannot reach absolute zero — and even there, atoms wiggle
items.claim: Absolute zero is 0 K, minus 273.15 degrees Celsius. The third law of thermodynamics says it's unattainable in finite steps. And even if you got there, atoms wouldn't stop moving.
items.prompt: Why can't atoms stop moving at 0 K?

options.text: Imperfect measurement makes them seem to move

Heisenberg uncertainty — atoms with zero kinetic energy would have zero momentum, but a perfectly known momentum implies infinite position uncertainty; the lowest-energy quantum state has irreducible 'zero-point' motion
Atoms always vibrate as long as they exist
Atoms keep moving due to cosmic background radiation

items.reveal_title: Zero-point energy — quantum residue at the bottom
items.reveal:
Every quantum oscillator has a ground-state energy of (1/2) h-bar omega above the bottom of its potential well. This isn't 'random' motion that can be removed — it's the lowest-energy state allowed by the uncertainty principle.

Helium remains liquid even at 0 K under normal pressure because zero-point motion is comparable to the inter-atomic binding energy — solidifying helium requires pressure to overcome it.

The third law of thermodynamics says you cannot reach 0 K in a finite number of steps: each cooling step removes a smaller and smaller fraction of remaining heat. Modern experiments have reached temperatures of around 100 picokelvin, but the laws of nature keep the last few degrees of headroom forever.
items.why: Absolute zero is imagined as 'no motion'. Quantum mechanics says even the ground state has motion — and you can never quite reach it anyway.

items.title: Astronauts on the ISS are not in zero gravity
items.claim: The International Space Station orbits about 400 km up. Earth's gravity there is still 89 percent of its surface value. Astronauts float not because gravity is absent but because both they and the station are in continual free fall.
items.prompt: If they're falling, why don't they hit Earth?

options.text: The station has engines that hold it up
They are falling — but also moving sideways at about 7.7 km/s, so the curvature of their trajectory matches the curvature of the Earth and they keep missing the ground
Gravity gets cancelled by the Moon
Air pressure at altitude keeps them up

items.reveal_title: Orbit is free fall that misses the Earth
items.reveal:
Newton's thought experiment: fire a cannonball horizontally from a mountaintop. Slow shots fall to Earth. At about 7.9 km/s, the cannonball falls fast enough that the Earth curves away beneath it at the same rate. It never lands — that's orbit.

The ISS is doing this constantly. The astronauts and the floors of the station are all accelerating toward Earth's centre at about 8.7 m/s squared — but in a circular path that misses the Earth.

Inside the station, since everything accelerates equally, nothing presses against anything else. The famous 'microgravity' isn't an absence of gravity — it's the equivalence of free fall and inertial motion that Einstein turned into the equivalence principle of general relativity.
items.why: Pop culture says astronauts are 'in zero gravity'. They're in nearly normal gravity but in continuous free fall. The two feel identical.

items.title: Lightning can hit your car and not hurt you
items.claim: A bolt of lightning carries 30,000 amps and a billion volts. Strike a car with you inside and you walk away (probably) unharmed. Not because rubber tyres insulate — they don't matter — but because of where the charge goes.
items.prompt: Why is the inside of the car safe?

options.text: Rubber tyres insulate from the ground

Charge on a conductor rests on its outer surface — the electric field inside a closed conducting shell is zero (the Faraday cage), so the inside of the car has no field even if the outside carries huge charge
Lightning prefers metal and skips the inside
The car's chassis is earthed to the road

items.reveal_title: Faraday cages — electrostatics' free safety equipment
items.reveal:
In electrostatic equilibrium, electric field inside a conductor is zero — free electrons would move to cancel it. Charge accumulates on the outer surface only. Any external field is screened.

A car shell is good enough for this purpose. Lightning hits the outside, runs around the shell, and jumps to ground from a wheel or fender. The interior remains nearly field-free.

Faraday demonstrated this dramatically in 1836 by sitting in a metallic cage while it was struck with sparks from an electrostatic machine. Microwave ovens (small holes in the door's metal mesh much smaller than microwave wavelength) and MRI rooms (RF-shielded cages) use the same principle every day.
items.why: Lightning safety is often misattributed to tyre insulation. The actual mechanism is electrostatic shielding by the car's conducting body.

items.title: A perfume molecule takes a very long time to reach the door
items.claim: Spritz perfume at one end of a still room. The molecules diffuse through the air. The mean speed of an air molecule is about 500 m/s. The perfume should cross a 5 m room in 10 milliseconds. It actually takes minutes to hours.
items.prompt: Why is diffusion so slow if individual molecules are so fast?

options.text: Diffusion has nothing to do with molecular motion
Each molecule collides with others about 10 to the 10 times per second, so it executes a random walk; mean displacement scales as the square root of time, not linearly
The perfume is heavier than air
Air resistance slows the molecules

items.reveal_title: Random walk — square-root scaling instead of linear
items.reveal:
Mean free path in air is about 70 nanometres. A perfume molecule's velocity changes direction roughly every 10 to the minus 10 seconds. Its position evolves as a random walk: net displacement after time t scales as the square root of (D times t), where D is the diffusion coefficient.

For air at room temperature D is about 10 to the minus 5 m squared per second. To cross 5 metres by diffusion: t equals 5 squared over D, which is roughly 2.5 million seconds — about a month.

In practice convection moves perfume around your room in seconds. Diffusion is far too slow for everyday scales. But it dominates inside cells (microns) — and over micron scales it takes only milliseconds.
items.why: Linear-time intuition for travel is wrong for random walks. Diffusion gets dramatically slower as scales increase, because of the square-root law.

items.title: The universe expands — and photons lose energy
items.claim: Light from a distant galaxy is redshifted. Its wavelength has stretched on the journey across the expanding universe. Lower frequency means lower photon energy (E equals hf). Where did the energy go?
items.prompt: Does cosmological redshift violate energy conservation?

options.text: No — the energy is transferred to space itself

Energy conservation in general relativity does not have to hold globally on cosmological scales — the symmetry (time-translation invariance) that gives rise to energy conservation is absent in an expanding universe
No — the photon's mass changes to compensate
Yes — energy conservation is just wrong

items.reveal:
Emmy Noether's 1918 theorem: every continuous symmetry of physical law gives rise to a conserved quantity. Time-translation symmetry gives conservation of energy.

Locally, spacetime has time-translation symmetry and energy is conserved beautifully. Globally, in an expanding universe, time-translation symmetry is broken — the universe is not the same today as it was a billion years ago. So the global statement of energy conservation simply does not apply in the form people learn in introductory classes.

The photon's energy goes 'nowhere' because there is no global energy to be accountable to. This is why some cosmologists say energy conservation in cosmology is at best subtle, at worst meaningless.
items.why: Energy conservation is taught as universal. In curved spacetime without a time symmetry, it isn't even well-defined globally.

items.title: Light 'chooses' the path that takes the least time
items.claim: Snell's law says n1 sin theta1 equals n2 sin theta2 at the interface between two media. This is also the path of least time. Light from A to B in air-then-water finds the unique path that minimises travel time.
items.prompt: Does light somehow 'know' the destination in advance?

options.text: Yes — light contains hidden information about the future

No — Fermat's principle is equivalent to local rules (Snell's law, derived from wave interference); all alternative paths have phases that approximately cancel, and only the path of stationary phase (the least-time one) survives
Yes — but only for visible light
No — the least-time path is a mathematical coincidence with no physical meaning

items.reveal_title: Stationary phase and the path integral
items.reveal:
Feynman's sum-over-histories formulation: light (or any quantum particle) doesn't take one path. It tries ALL paths. Each path contributes an amplitude with a phase determined by the action along that path.

For paths far from the classical (Fermat) path, neighbouring paths have wildly different phases and cancel out by interference. Near the Fermat path, the phase is stationary — nearby paths have nearly the same phase and add up constructively.

The observable outcome is dominated by the path of stationary action. For light, that path is the one of stationary travel time. Snell's law isn't a magical 'choice' — it's the consequence of constructive interference among many paths.
items.why: Variational principles ('the system finds the optimal path') look mystical. They're really shorthand for interference effects among all possible paths.

items.title: A hammer and a feather fall at the same rate — on the Moon
items.claim: In 1971, Apollo 15 commander David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather on the lunar surface. With no air, they hit the ground simultaneously. On Earth, the feather drifts.
items.prompt: Why are objects in vacuum equally accelerated regardless of mass?

options.text: Mass cancels in gravity but not in air resistance — F equals mg gives a equals g for all masses, independent of m
Heavier objects fall faster, as Aristotle taught
The Moon's lower gravity equalises everything
Atoms of equal mass act equally regardless of vacuum

items.reveal_title: Equivalence of gravitational and inertial mass
items.reveal:
Newton's second law: F equals ma. Gravity: F equals m sub g times g, where m sub g is the gravitational mass. Setting them equal: a equals (m sub g over m sub i) times g. If gravitational mass equals inertial mass — and to date no experiment has distinguished them, to better than 1 part in 10 to the 13 (MICROSCOPE satellite, 2017) — then a equals g for all bodies.

Galileo allegedly demonstrated this from the Leaning Tower of Pisa (his student Viviani says so; the historical record is unclear). The Apollo 15 demonstration is recorded on video and unambiguous.

Einstein elevated the equivalence to a principle and built general relativity on top of it: gravity is geometry, and all objects in free fall follow the same geodesic regardless of mass.
items.why: Daily observation (feathers float, rocks drop) suggests heavier things fall faster. Air resistance is doing the work — gravity treats them all equally.

items.title: Sound travels four times faster in water than in air
items.claim: Sound moves at about 343 m/s in air. In water, it moves at about 1480 m/s. In steel, it moves at 5000 m/s. Denser materials slow sound, surely? No — denser is faster, if the stiffness scales properly.
items.prompt: Why is sound faster in steel than in air?

options.text: Steel atoms vibrate faster
Sound speed equals the square root of (elastic modulus divided by density); steel's stiffness vastly outweighs its density, giving a much higher ratio than air's
Steel has no gaps between atoms, so sound transmits instantly
Sound in steel uses light to propagate

items.reveal:
Sound is a mechanical wave. Its speed in a medium depends on how much restoring force is generated per unit strain (bulk modulus, K) divided by how massive the displaced material is (density, rho). v equals the square root of K over rho.

Air: K about 1.4 times 10 to the 5 Pa, rho about 1.2 kg per cubic metre. Ratio gives 343 m/s.
Water: K about 2.2 times 10 to the 9 Pa, rho 1000 kg per cubic metre. Ratio gives 1480 m/s.
Steel: K about 1.6 times 10 to the 11 Pa, rho 7800 kg per cubic metre. Ratio gives 5000 m/s.

Density slows things down per unit force; stiffness speeds things up per unit displacement. Steel is much stiffer than air relative to its density.
items.why: Intuition says heavier is harder to move and so slower. The full picture includes how hard the material resists deformation, not just its mass.

items.title: Edison lost the war of currents in the 1890s
items.claim: Thomas Edison championed direct current (DC) for distributing electricity. George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla pushed alternating current (AC). By 1895 AC had won — and every domestic supply on Earth is now AC for a single decisive technical reason.
items.prompt: Why did AC beat DC for power distribution?

options.text: AC is safer to touch

AC can be stepped up to very high voltage (low current) for long-distance transmission and stepped back down for domestic use using transformers — DC cannot easily be transformed, so it loses huge amounts of energy as heat in distribution cables
Edison's patents expired
DC produces more harmful magnetic fields

items.reveal_title: Power dissipation scales as I squared R
items.reveal:
Power loss in a transmission line is I squared times R. For a given power delivered (P = VI), higher voltage means lower current, and so vastly lower losses. Transformers (Faraday's induction, 1831) require an alternating magnetic flux — AC works, DC does not.

UK grid runs at 50 Hz; US, Mexico, parts of Brazil run at 60 Hz. The choice was historical (early generators in Europe vs America had different design constants) and is now too embedded to change.

High-voltage DC transmission HAS become possible since the 1950s (solid-state converters) and is now used for very long undersea cables. But local distribution to homes is still AC because that's what every appliance and wall socket has been built around.
items.why: AC's dominance is taught as a historical fact. The deeper reason is the I squared R loss in transmission combined with transformers' need for changing flux.

items.title: Transformers can be over 99 percent efficient — better than almost any machine
items.claim: A large power-station step-up transformer is around 99.5 percent efficient. A typical car engine is about 25 percent. Most domestic appliances are 30-80 percent. Transformers convert AC voltage with almost no loss.
items.prompt: How is a passive iron-and-copper device so efficient?

options.text: It contains no moving parts to wear out

Transformers have no thermodynamic Carnot limit because they don't go via heat — they exchange energy magnetically by mutual induction; losses are limited to ohmic heating in windings, eddy currents and core hysteresis
They store energy and return it later
They use superconducting wire

items.reveal:
A transformer has two coils wound around a shared iron core. AC in the primary creates an oscillating magnetic flux through the core; the flux induces an EMF in the secondary equal to V_secondary = (N_secondary / N_primary) × V_primary.

Losses come from: (1) ohmic heating in the windings (I squared R), (2) eddy currents induced in the iron core (suppressed by laminating the core into thin insulated sheets), (3) hysteresis losses as the iron magnetises and demagnetises 100 times per second (50 Hz, both polarities).

A well-designed transformer at full load loses about 0.5 percent. Empty (no load on secondary), losses fall to a fraction of a percent. The same physics underlies wireless phone chargers — inductive coupling at higher frequencies.
items.why: Transformers look passive and boring. They are among the most efficient energy-conversion devices humans have ever built.

items.title: Metals get MORE resistive when heated; semiconductors get LESS
items.claim: Heat a copper wire and its resistance rises by about 0.4 percent per degree Celsius. Heat a semiconductor (like a thermistor) and its resistance falls dramatically. The two materials respond oppositely to temperature.
items.prompt: Why do metals and semiconductors behave oppositely?

options.text: Metals expand and semiconductors contract

In metals, increased temperature means more lattice vibrations (phonons) that scatter conduction electrons, raising resistance. In semiconductors, increased temperature liberates more charge carriers across the band gap, lowering resistance
Semiconductors melt at lower temperatures
The two have opposite signs of electric charge

items.reveal:
In a metal, the conduction electron density is essentially fixed (one or two per atom). Resistance is dominated by how often electrons scatter off lattice vibrations — more heat means more phonons, more scattering, more resistance. This is a positive temperature coefficient (PTC).

In an intrinsic semiconductor, conduction requires electrons (or holes) to be thermally excited across a band gap. The number of carriers rises exponentially with temperature (n ∝ exp(-Eg/2kT)). The carrier density swamps the scattering and resistance falls — a negative temperature coefficient (NTC).

NTC thermistors are used in temperature sensors (precision better than 0.1°C). PTC thermistors are used as self-resetting fuses — runaway heating raises their resistance and limits current.
items.why: Resistance is treated as a fixed property of a wire. It depends on which carriers are available — and that depends on temperature in very different ways for metals and semiconductors.

items.title: Wet skin is 100 times more conductive than dry skin
items.claim: Dry skin has a resistance of around 100,000 ohms. Wet skin drops to about 1000 ohms — a factor of 100. A 240 V shock that you would barely feel through dry hands could be lethal through wet ones.
items.prompt: Why does moisture matter so much for electrical safety?

options.text: Water generates extra voltage

The outer keratin layer of dry skin is a poor conductor; moisture (sweat, rain, soapy water) fills in pores and creates ionic conduction paths, dropping skin resistance by orders of magnitude and increasing the current that flows for a given voltage
Water is more attractive to lightning
Water makes skin elastic and so harder to insulate

items.reveal_title: Ohm's law and the human body
items.reveal:
Current through the body: I = V / R. At 240 V (UK mains) through dry hands (R ~ 100,000 ohms): I = 2.4 mA — barely noticeable. Same voltage through wet hands (R ~ 1000 ohms): I = 240 mA — fatal in seconds.

The threshold of perception is about 1 mA. 'Let-go threshold' (when muscles spasm and you can't release the conductor) is 10-20 mA. Ventricular fibrillation starts above ~50 mA passed through the chest. Death is rapid above 100 mA.

This is why bathrooms have special wiring rules, why you don't operate electrical appliances with wet hands, and why mains supply to wet areas runs through RCDs that detect imbalances of a few mA and cut the supply within milliseconds.
items.why: Voltage alone doesn't determine danger. Current through the body depends on skin resistance, which can change by 100 times depending on dampness.

items.title: A lightning bolt carries 30,000 amps at 100 million volts
items.claim: A typical cloud-to-ground lightning strike delivers around 30 kA of current at about 100 MV, lasting roughly 30 microseconds. Total energy: around 1 gigajoule — enough to power a 100 W bulb for 100 days.
items.prompt: Where does the megavolt potential difference come from?

options.text: Cosmic rays charge the cloud
Collisions between rising water droplets and falling ice within thunderclouds transfer charge, building up a charge separation of perhaps 100 megavolts between cloud and ground over many minutes
Earth's magnetic field induces the voltage
The Sun directly charges the cloud

items.reveal:
Thunderclouds are not fully understood, but the leading mechanism involves graupel (soft hail) falling through a cloud of supercooled water droplets and ice crystals. Collisions transfer electrons preferentially, leaving the cloud's lower regions strongly negative and the top positive.

When the field between cloud and ground exceeds air's breakdown strength (about 3 MV/m, varying with humidity), a stepped leader runs down from the cloud and a return stroke runs up from the ground. The visible 'bolt' is the return stroke — peak currents around 30 kA, lasting tens of microseconds.

The accompanying heating turns air into a plasma briefly at temperatures of 30,000 K — five times the Sun's surface temperature. The expansion is the thunderclap.
items.why: Lightning gets taught as 'static electricity writ large'. The voltages and currents involved are at the extreme limit of what electromagnetic theory describes — and the bolt itself is plasma physics.

items.title: An RCD doesn't measure how big the current is — it measures whether currents balance
items.claim: A fuse blows when current rises too high. A residual current device (RCD or ground-fault circuit interrupter) does something different: it measures the difference between current going OUT on the live wire and current returning on the neutral. Any imbalance over about 30 mA trips the device in 25 ms.
items.prompt: Why measure imbalance rather than total current?

options.text: Imbalance is easier to measure

In a healthy circuit, current out equals current back. If any current is leaking to earth (through a person, a faulty appliance, water in a socket), the two no longer balance — and that's exactly the dangerous condition a fuse can't detect
Fuses are unreliable
Imbalance currents are illegal

items.reveal:
The live and neutral wires both pass through a small toroidal core inside the RCD. If equal current flows in opposite directions, their magnetic fields cancel exactly — no signal. If a fraction leaks to earth (say, through a person touching a live wire), the currents no longer cancel and a net magnetic flux is induced through the core.

A small sensing coil picks up the imbalance and triggers a fast electromechanical switch. UK regulations require trip thresholds of 30 mA or less and trip times under 40 ms for socket circuits in dwellings.

Fuses protect against the wires overheating (overcurrent); RCDs protect against the person being electrocuted (earth leakage). Modern installations combine them as RCBOs.
items.why: Safety devices are taught as 'fuses prevent fires'. RCDs and earth wires together prevent the more common cause of injury — leakage current through a human body.

items.title: UK ring circuits split current down two paths
items.claim: UK domestic socket circuits are wired as a 'ring' — the cable leaves the consumer unit, runs around the room from socket to socket, and returns to the same circuit breaker. Current splits and runs both ways around the loop.
items.prompt: Why this unusual topology?

options.text: Aesthetics
Each cable carries half the load, so thinner cable can serve a higher total load — a 32 A ring uses 2.5 mm² cable instead of the 6 mm² that would be needed for a radial circuit of the same capacity
Ring circuits cannot trip a fuse
Rings produce a stronger magnetic field for induction cooking

items.reveal:
In a radial circuit, all current flows down a single cable. A 32 A load needs cable rated for 32 A — typically 6 mm² copper.

In a ring circuit, current can divide. If the load is balanced near the middle of the ring, each leg carries about 16 A — so 2.5 mm² cable suffices. The ring also gives redundancy: if one leg is broken, the other can still carry the (reduced) load.

This economy of copper became important during post-war shortages in Britain. Other countries didn't adopt the system. Modern criticism of ring circuits centres on the difficulty of testing them and the risk of imbalance if connections are degraded — but they remain standard in UK domestic wiring.
items.why: Wiring topology is taught as plumbing diagrams. The UK ring is a historical and engineering choice that traded redundancy and copper economy against testing complexity.

items.title: The third pin in a UK plug is doing almost nothing — until something fails
items.claim: In a properly working appliance, no current flows in the earth wire. It is connected to the metal casing of the appliance and to ground via the consumer unit. In normal operation, it does nothing visible.
items.prompt: Why install a wire that normally does nothing?

options.text: Aesthetic balance with the other pins

If a fault occurs and live wire touches the metal casing, the earth wire gives a low-resistance path to ground — drawing a huge current that immediately blows the fuse or trips the RCD, before a person touching the casing can be shocked
The earth wire reduces electromagnetic interference
The earth wire grounds the appliance to prevent static buildup

items.reveal:
Consider a kettle. The metal body is connected to the earth pin. Internally, the live wire is insulated and connected to the heating element. If the insulation fails and the live wire contacts the body, the body becomes live at 240 V — potentially lethal to anyone touching the kettle.

But with the earth wire in place, the contact creates a near-short circuit through the earth wire to ground. Current rises to hundreds of amps almost instantly — blowing the fuse or tripping the RCD within milliseconds.

Class II appliances ('double insulated', square within a square symbol) have insulation thick enough that there is no exposed metal that could become live — they don't need an earth and use only two-pin plugs.
items.why: The earth wire is taught as 'safety' but its mechanism is specifically to convert a dangerous fault into a current spike that protective devices can detect.

items.title: Devices on standby cost the world about 1 percent of total electricity
items.claim: TVs, set-top boxes, microwaves, phone chargers and printers continue to draw current even when 'off'. The International Energy Agency estimated this 'phantom load' or 'vampire power' at about 1 percent of global electricity consumption — roughly 250 TWh per year.
items.prompt: Why does a device draw power when you've turned it off?

options.text: The plug leaks current
The device keeps a remote-control receiver, clock, memory or network interface powered — typically through a small transformer that wastes a few watts continuously
Electricity meters are inaccurate at low currents
Heat from the wires keeps the device warm

items.reveal:
A typical TV on standby draws 1-5 W. A printer 2-10 W. A microwave with a clock 1-3 W. Phone chargers without a phone 0.1-1 W. A wifi router can draw 5-15 W around the clock.

Average UK household has 15-20 always-on devices. Total standby load can reach 50-100 W continuously — about 500-1000 kWh per year, costing £100-200.

EU regulations now cap standby consumption: most products must use under 0.5 W in standby. Newer designs use 'soft-off' switches that genuinely cut almost all current. The simplest fix is unplugging or using switched extension leads.
items.why: 'Off' is not zero. Small persistent loads multiplied by billions of devices add up to a percentage of global energy use.

items.title: The UK grid frequency is controlled to better than 0.1 percent — and powers some clocks
items.claim: UK mains is 50 Hz. The National Grid maintains this to ±1 percent in normal operation, and long-term averages to better than 0.01 percent. Older mechanical clocks plugged into the wall count grid cycles and so are accurate to within a few seconds per year.
items.prompt: Why is the grid frequency held so precisely?

options.text: To keep mains clocks accurate

All generators on the grid must run synchronously — frequency is set by the rotational speed of the generators, and any imbalance between supply and demand causes the frequency to drift. Holding it close to 50 Hz proves supply matches demand
Higher frequencies waste energy
50 Hz is the resonant frequency of most appliances

items.reveal_title: Frequency as a signal of grid balance
items.reveal:
Synchronous generators across the country are all locked in phase. They rotate at speeds set by 50 Hz × pole-pair count. If demand exceeds supply, the generators slow down a tiny amount — frequency dips. National Grid responds by ramping up generation (or load shedding).

The famous 9 August 2019 UK blackout started with a frequency dip after lightning hit a gas plant. Frequency fell from 50 Hz to 48.8 Hz in 9 seconds. About 1 million homes lost power.

Europe's continental grid runs at 50 Hz too. Britain, Ireland and Iceland are connected to it asynchronously via HVDC interconnectors. A grid-synchronisation event between Europe and Africa in 2021 momentarily linked their frequencies — a rare and dramatic technical feat.
items.why: Mains frequency is taught as 'a number'. It's a continuously updated balance signal between supply and demand for an entire country's power system.

items.title: Earth's magnetic field is feeble — about 50 microtesla at the surface
items.claim: A typical fridge magnet generates a field of about 5 millitesla at its surface — about 100 times stronger than Earth's field. The field that swings every compass and protects life from solar wind is barely measurable with everyday instruments.
items.prompt: How does such a weak field deflect cosmic rays and the solar wind?

options.text: Charged particles are easily deflected by even weak fields when no other forces apply
Earth's field is much stronger than 50 microtesla in space
The deflection is from the atmosphere, not the magnetic field
The Sun's field cancels in the upper atmosphere

items.reveal_title: Lorentz force on a fast charged particle
items.reveal:
Earth's field at the surface is about 25-65 microtesla, depending on latitude. The field weakens with the cube of distance from the centre (it's nearly a magnetic dipole), so at the magnetopause (about 60,000 km out on the day side) it's down to a few nanotesla.

A proton in the solar wind has speed about 400 km/s. The Lorentz force qv × B is significant: gyroradius (the size of the circular path around a magnetic field line) is about 60 m for a typical solar wind proton near Earth — small compared with planetary scales. So charged particles spiral along field lines rather than crossing them.

The magnetosphere deflects the solar wind around Earth, funnels some particles to the poles (where they collide with the atmosphere and produce auroras), and traps high-energy particles in the Van Allen belts.
items.why: Earth's field 'feels' strong because it moves compasses noticeably. In tesla units it is millions of times weaker than an MRI scanner — but enough to deflect the solar wind.

items.title: Heat iron past 770°C and it stops being magnetic
items.claim: Iron is the iconic ferromagnet. But heat it above 770°C (its Curie temperature) and it loses all permanent magnetism. Cool it below 770°C and ferromagnetism returns spontaneously.
items.prompt: What happens to the magnetism at the Curie temperature?

options.text: The atoms melt and lose their magnetic moments

Thermal motion above the Curie temperature is energetic enough to disrupt the alignment of magnetic moments in domains; below it, exchange interactions between neighbouring atoms force alignment and macroscopic magnetisation emerges
The iron releases its electrons
Magnetic moments evaporate at high temperature

items.reveal:
Each iron atom has a magnetic moment from unpaired electron spins. Quantum-mechanical exchange interactions between neighbouring atoms favour parallel alignment, producing tiny ordered regions called domains.

Below the Curie temperature (Tc = 1043 K = 770°C for iron, 1394 K for cobalt, 631 K for nickel), the exchange energy beats thermal disruption and domains exist. Above Tc, thermal energy overwhelms exchange and the spins point in random directions — the material becomes paramagnetic.

This is a second-order phase transition. Magnetic susceptibility diverges near Tc, magnetisation rises sharply just below Tc, and the heat capacity has a characteristic lambda-shaped peak.

Forging blacksmiths know iron passes through a 'critical point' as it cools — a sudden change in feel and colour at around Tc.
items.why: Magnetism is taught as a fixed property of iron. It is a phase that exists only below a certain temperature.

items.title: An MRI scanner uses a 1.5 tesla magnetic field — 30,000 times Earth's
items.claim: A typical clinical MRI scanner has a magnetic field around 1.5 T; high-field research machines reach 7 T. Generating such a field continuously requires kilometres of niobium-titanium wire cooled by liquid helium to about 4 K, where it becomes superconducting and carries current with no losses.
items.prompt: Why are superconducting magnets used instead of ordinary electromagnets?

options.text: Superconductors are cheap

An ordinary copper-wire electromagnet generating 1.5 T over the bore needed for a patient would dissipate megawatts of heat — practical only for brief pulses; a superconducting magnet, once energised, carries the same current forever with essentially no power input
Superconductors produce stronger fields per amp
Liquid helium is required for the radio detection

items.reveal:
A superconducting magnet is energised once (the current is ramped up from zero) and the current loop is closed via a superconducting switch. The current then flows indefinitely with no resistive losses. The magnet maintains its field as long as the helium keeps the wire below its critical temperature.

Liquid helium boils away slowly. A clinical MRI typically uses a 'cold head' refrigerator to recondense escaping helium — losses are then near zero for years. A 'quench' (loss of superconductivity, often from a tiny warm spot) dumps the magnet's stored energy as heat in seconds, boiling the helium and venting it through emergency pipes.

MRI uses the magnetic field to align protons in the patient's tissue; radio-frequency pulses tip the alignment; relaxation back to the field emits signals that are spatially reconstructed into images.
items.why: Superconductivity is taught as a cryogenic curiosity. It is the technology that makes medical MRI imaging possible — and many particle accelerators.

items.title: Cut a bar magnet in half and you get TWO bar magnets — never an isolated pole
items.claim: Electric charges come in two flavours: positive and negative, and they can exist alone. Magnets always have a north pole AND a south pole. Cut a magnet in half and each half is itself a complete magnet. Cut again — same result. No 'magnetic monopole' has ever been detected.
items.prompt: Does that mean monopoles cannot exist?

options.text: Yes — magnetic field lines must always form closed loops

Maxwell's equations currently encode no magnetic charge, but Dirac showed in 1931 that the EXISTENCE of monopoles would explain electric charge quantisation; many theories beyond the Standard Model predict monopoles. They are simply not observed
Yes — monopoles would violate energy conservation
No — they exist but are too small to detect

items.reveal_title: The empirical asymmetry of electricity and magnetism
items.reveal:
Maxwell's equations have ∇·E = ρ/ε0 (electric monopoles — charges — are real) and ∇·B = 0 (no magnetic monopoles). The second is empirical, not theoretical: it just describes what we observe.

Dirac (1931) showed that if even one magnetic monopole existed anywhere in the universe, the quantisation of electric charge in units of e would follow as a mathematical consequence. Why don't we see them?

Grand unified theories predict monopoles formed in the early universe and have mass around 10 to the 16 GeV — way beyond the LHC. Cosmic ray detectors and proton-decay experiments have searched, with no confirmed sighting. The Cabrera 1982 'Valentine's Day' single-event remains the only candidate detection — never reproduced.

Magnetic analogues of monopole behaviour have been observed in solid-state systems (spin ices) but those are emergent quasi-particles, not fundamental.
items.why: Electromagnetic symmetry is taught as if it were complete. The asymmetry between electric and magnetic monopoles is one of physics' open empirical puzzles.

items.title: The minus sign in Faraday's law saves energy conservation
items.claim: Faraday's law of induction: EMF = -dΦ/dt. The minus sign (Lenz's law) says the induced current always opposes the change that caused it. Drop a magnet through a copper tube and it falls slowly because the induced currents brake it.
items.prompt: Why must the sign be negative?

options.text: Convention only — physics works either way

If the induced current reinforced the change in flux, energy would be created from nothing: a falling magnet would accelerate, induce stronger currents, accelerate more — a runaway. Conservation of energy requires the induced current to OPPOSE the change
Maxwell wrote it that way to be consistent with his other equations
It's a quirk of the right-hand rule

items.reveal:
Drop a strong neodymium magnet through a copper pipe. The magnet's motion changes magnetic flux through circular cross-sections of the copper. Induced eddy currents oppose the flux change — the induced current creates a magnetic field opposing the magnet's approach, then opposing its departure.

The forces between the magnet and induced currents brake the fall. Gravitational potential energy is dissipated as heat in the copper. A neodymium magnet can take 10+ seconds to fall through a metre of copper pipe — instead of less than half a second in free fall.

If Lenz's law were reversed, the magnet would accelerate AND induce stronger currents that further accelerated it. Kinetic energy would grow without limit from nowhere. The minus sign is energy conservation, written as a vector equation.
items.why: The minus sign looks like an arbitrary convention. It is the algebraic statement that energy cannot be created from electromagnetic induction.

items.title: Auroras are the atmosphere being hit by 100 km/s electrons from the Sun
items.claim: The northern and southern lights are produced when high-energy electrons (and to a lesser extent protons) from the solar wind are funnelled along Earth's magnetic field lines into the upper atmosphere. They collide with oxygen and nitrogen atoms, exciting them; the atoms emit characteristic colours as they relax.
items.prompt: Why are auroras seen near the poles, not the equator?

options.text: The atmosphere is thinner there
Charged particles trapped by Earth's magnetic field spiral along field lines, and field lines converge into the polar regions — that's where particles meet the atmosphere
The Sun aims its wind preferentially at the poles
Cold weather is required for auroras

items.reveal_title: Charged particles trapped by a dipole
items.reveal:
Earth's magnetic field is roughly a dipole. Field lines emerge near the south magnetic pole, loop through space, and enter near the north magnetic pole. Charged particles spiralling along these lines mirror back and forth between hemispheres, trapped in the Van Allen belts.

During solar storms, dense bursts of energetic electrons stream down field lines into the upper atmosphere at altitudes of 100-300 km. The electrons collide with O and N atoms and excite their electrons; on relaxation, photons emerge at characteristic wavelengths.

Oxygen at low altitude (100 km) gives the familiar green emission line at 558 nm. Oxygen at high altitude (>200 km) gives a rare red emission at 630 nm. Nitrogen contributes blue and purple. The colour distribution traces altitude, particle energy and atmospheric composition.

Auroras have been observed on Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — every planet with a magnetic field.
items.why: Auroras are taught as a 'pretty light show'. They are emission spectra of the upper atmosphere lit up by solar-wind electrons, mapped by the geometry of Earth's magnetic field.

items.title: Heat and temperature are different things
items.claim: A burning sparkler reaches 1000°C. A cup of hot tea is at 80°C. Touching the sparkler causes no damage; touching the tea would scald you. Yet the sparkler is much hotter.
items.prompt: Why does the cooler tea cause more damage?

options.text: Tea is more corrosive

Temperature measures the average kinetic energy per particle; heat (energy transferred) depends on temperature, mass and specific heat capacity. A cup of tea has a huge total heat content compared to a few sparks of iron
Sparklers cool faster
Tea is more conductive than sparks

items.reveal:
A sparkler's molten iron particles are at high temperature (high kinetic energy per atom) but the total mass is tiny — a few milligrams. Total heat: 0.001 kg × 460 J/kg·K × 1000 K ≈ 0.5 J.

A cup of tea is at lower temperature but contains 250 g of water. Total heat above body temperature: 0.25 × 4180 × 40 ≈ 42,000 J — about 100,000 times more.

Damage to skin depends on how much heat is delivered before equilibrium, which depends on total heat content and contact area. A drop of liquid metal delivers a brief, intense local heating but small total energy; a cup of tea delivers sustained heat over a larger area.

This is why some materials (low specific heat capacity, low mass) feel hot to touch but don't burn you, while others (high specific heat, high mass) can scald at much lower temperatures.
items.why: Heat and temperature are often used interchangeably. They are mathematically and physically distinct quantities — and the difference matters for safety.

items.title: A vacuum flask works by blocking three different things at once
items.claim: A Thermos flask keeps coffee hot for hours by simultaneously blocking conduction (vacuum gap), convection (no air to circulate), and radiation (silvered inner walls). Each mechanism alone wouldn't be enough.
items.prompt: Why is each layer needed?

options.text: Redundancy in case one fails

The three heat-transfer mechanisms operate by different physical processes; blocking only one allows the others to dominate. The vacuum eliminates conduction and convection through air; the silvered walls reflect infrared radiation back into the contents
Conduction is the slowest by itself
Each layer cools a different temperature range

items.reveal:
Conduction: kinetic energy transferred between atoms in contact. Best blocked by removing matter (vacuum) or using poor thermal conductors (foam, fibreglass).

Convection: bulk movement of fluid carrying heat. Best blocked by removing the fluid or preventing flow (sealed cells, vacuum).

Radiation: infrared electromagnetic waves emitted by warm surfaces. Best blocked by reflective (low-emissivity) surfaces or by interposing reflective layers.

A vacuum flask combines all three: the vacuum gap suppresses conduction and convection between inner and outer walls; the silvered inner surface reflects infrared back to the contents instead of letting it radiate out. Modern double-walled stainless steel travel mugs do the same.

Space blankets exploit the radiation channel — a thin metallised film reflects up to 97 percent of body radiation back at the wearer.
items.why: Heat transfer is taught as three separate topics. Real insulation problems require considering all three at once — and a vacuum flask is the classic case.

items.title: Water has the highest specific heat of any common liquid
items.claim: Raising the temperature of 1 kg of water by 1°C requires 4180 J. The same energy raises 1 kg of iron by 9.3°C, 1 kg of mercury by 30°C. Water is exceptionally hard to warm — and to cool.
items.prompt: What makes water's heat capacity so high?

options.text: Water is a polar molecule

Heat in water is shared between molecular vibrations, rotations, and the breaking and re-forming of hydrogen bonds; the hydrogen-bond network absorbs huge amounts of energy with only modest temperature rise
Water is denser than most liquids
Water has free electrons

items.reveal:
When you heat water, energy doesn't just speed molecules up. A significant fraction goes into stretching and breaking hydrogen bonds — about 23 kJ/mol per bond, with each molecule forming up to four.

This is why coastal climates are mild: oceans absorb and release heat slowly. The Gulf Stream warms northwest Europe by carrying tropical heat north. Water's heat capacity buffers the climate.

It's also why sweating cools so effectively: evaporating 1 g of water absorbs 2260 J (latent heat of vaporisation) — far more than the same mass of any common solvent. And why ice cubes drop drinks' temperatures so quickly: melting 1 g of ice absorbs 334 J (latent heat of fusion).
items.why: Specific heat is taught as a number to look up. It is a measure of how many ways a substance can absorb energy at the molecular level.

items.title: You cannot reach absolute zero in finite steps
items.claim: Absolute zero is 0 K, -273.15°C. The third law of thermodynamics says you cannot reach it in a finite number of cooling steps. Modern experiments have got to 38 picokelvin — but the last few degrees stay out of reach forever.
items.prompt: Why is the bottom unreachable?

options.text: Equipment cannot handle such low temperatures
Each cooling step removes a smaller and smaller fraction of remaining heat (each reduction of entropy gets harder). Reaching exactly S = 0 would require an infinite number of steps
Heat keeps flowing in from the universe
Atoms melt at very low temperature

items.reveal:
Cooling techniques like adiabatic demagnetisation can lower the temperature of a substance in stages. Each stage requires removing some of the system's entropy. The Nernst-Simon statement of the third law: as T → 0, the entropy of any reversible process approaches a constant, and the rate of cooling per stage falls toward zero.

In practice, the gap from millikelvin to nanokelvin requires entirely different techniques (dilution refrigerators, then laser cooling, then evaporative cooling of trapped atom clouds).

The lowest measured temperature in a lab is about 38 picokelvin (Bremen, 2021). The cosmic microwave background sits at 2.725 K. The coldest natural place known is the Boomerang Nebula at about 1 K.

Even at 0 K, atoms have zero-point motion required by the uncertainty principle — they cannot be truly still.
items.why: Absolute zero is taught as a fixed point on the scale. It is an unreachable asymptote, both thermodynamically and quantum-mechanically.

items.title: You can tell a star's temperature from its colour
items.claim: Red stars are cool (around 3000 K). Yellow-white stars like our Sun are medium (about 5800 K). Blue-white stars are hot (around 30,000 K). The peak wavelength of light shifts predictably with temperature — Wien's displacement law.
items.prompt: Why does a body's emission spectrum depend on its temperature?

options.text: Different elements give different colours
Any opaque body in thermal equilibrium emits a black-body spectrum determined only by its temperature (Planck's law). Wien: λ_max × T = 2.898 × 10 to the minus 3 m·K
Hotter objects emit more colours
Cooler objects emit only invisible light

items.reveal_title: Planck's law and the universality of the curve
items.reveal:
Any opaque body in thermal equilibrium emits radiation across a spectrum that depends only on its temperature — independent of material composition. The spectrum peaks at a wavelength λ_max = 2.898 × 10 to the minus 3 / T metres.

Human body at 310 K: peaks at about 9.3 μm (mid-IR — what thermal cameras see).
Incandescent bulb filament at 2800 K: peaks at about 1.04 μm (near-IR, with significant visible — yellow).
Sun at 5800 K: peaks at about 500 nm (visible green-yellow).
Blue O-class star at 30,000 K: peaks at about 97 nm (UV).

Total radiated power scales as T to the 4 (Stefan-Boltzmann). Doubling the temperature gives 16 times the radiation. This is why hot stars dominate galactic light output even though they are rarer than cool ones.
items.why: Star colours are taught as 'fun fact'. They are precise measurements of surface temperature based on a universal quantum-statistical curve.

items.title: Without the greenhouse effect, Earth would be -18°C on average
items.claim: Earth absorbs sunlight at visible wavelengths and re-emits energy as infrared. Greenhouse gases (water vapour, CO2, methane) absorb infrared on its way out and re-radiate it in all directions — including back to the surface. Without this effect Earth's mean surface temperature would be about -18°C; with it, the actual mean is about 15°C.
items.prompt: Why does an atmospheric trace gas matter so much?

options.text: It absorbs all sunlight
Greenhouse gases are largely transparent to visible light (which reaches the surface) but opaque to thermal infrared (which the surface emits) — this asymmetry traps energy in the lower atmosphere
It produces heat by combustion
It reflects sunlight back

items.reveal_title: Asymmetric absorption of visible vs infrared
items.reveal:
Sunlight peaks in the visible (about 500 nm). Earth's surface, at about 288 K, emits in the mid-infrared (peaking around 10 μm). Greenhouse gases (H2O, CO2, CH4, N2O, O3) have vibration modes that resonate with mid-IR but not visible light.

The consequence: sunlight gets in easily; the re-emitted infrared is partly absorbed and re-radiated back down. The lower atmosphere warms.

Pre-industrial CO2: about 280 ppm. Current (2024): about 425 ppm. The added CO2 doesn't dominate by mass — water vapour is far more abundant — but it's a knob humans can turn. Every doubling of CO2 raises equilibrium temperature by an estimated 2.5-4°C (climate sensitivity), with feedbacks (water vapour, ice albedo, clouds) accounting for most of the response.

Without any greenhouse effect at all, Earth would have a mean surface temperature similar to the Moon's: -18°C, with seas frozen solid.
items.why: The greenhouse effect is taught as 'CO2 bad'. The mechanism (selective infrared absorption) is what makes it both an essential planetary process and a climate-change concern.

items.title: Repeating a measurement reduces one kind of error but not another
items.claim: Measure a length with a ruler 10 times and average — the result is more reliable than any single measurement. Measure with an uncalibrated ruler 10,000 times and the average is still wrong.
items.prompt: Why does averaging help with random error but not systematic error?

options.text: Averaging is mathematical magic

Random errors fluctuate around the true value and partially cancel when averaged (uncertainty falls as 1/√N). Systematic errors shift every measurement in the same direction by the same amount — averaging does nothing
Systematic errors are smaller than random errors
Averaging amplifies systematic errors

items.reveal:
Random error: unpredictable fluctuations around the true value. Sources: meniscus reading, parallax, sensor noise, vibration. Averaging N independent measurements reduces the standard error by a factor of √N.

Systematic error: every measurement shifted by the same amount in the same direction. Sources: uncalibrated instrument, zero offset, observer bias, faulty technique. Averaging doesn't help.

Good practice: repeat measurements to reduce random error, then calibrate against a known standard to detect systematic error. Report both. Modern lab work distinguishes 'repeatability' (one operator, one instrument, same day) from 'reproducibility' (different operators, different instruments, different days) — they catch different sources of error.
items.why: Students take averages without thinking about which errors averaging can and cannot fix. Real precision needs different techniques for different error types.

items.title: Significant figures are a sloppy short-hand for uncertainty
items.claim: Quoting a length as 3.14 m suggests it lies between 3.135 m and 3.145 m. Quoting it as 3.140 m narrows that to 3.1395 to 3.1405. Significant figures encode uncertainty but only approximately and discontinuously.
items.prompt: What does a precise measurement actually look like?

options.text: Many decimal places
A central value with an explicit uncertainty: 3.140 ± 0.002 m. This makes the precision claim mathematically clear and propagates through subsequent calculations
Whole numbers
Calibrated against a known unit only

items.reveal:
Significant figures are a quick shorthand. Real precision quotes uncertainty explicitly: 3.140 ± 0.002 m, or with a percentage (3.140 m ± 0.06 percent), or with a confidence interval (e.g. '95 percent confidence').

When combining measurements, uncertainties combine: addition/subtraction adds absolute uncertainties in quadrature; multiplication/division adds relative uncertainties in quadrature.

Resolution (the smallest difference an instrument can distinguish — often the smallest division on a scale) is not the same as uncertainty. A ruler with 1 mm markings has 1 mm resolution but its uncertainty in a typical reading might be ±0.5 mm at best — and worse if it's bent or warped.
items.why: Sig figs are taught as a rounding rule. They are a coarse encoding of precision; explicit ± uncertainty is the professional approach.

items.title: Every measurement in a working lab traces back to seven international standards
items.claim: Every length, mass, temperature, current, time, light intensity and amount of substance measurement at any modern lab can be traced through calibration chains back to seven defined units maintained by international bodies. Calibration is what makes measurements comparable across labs.
items.prompt: What does 'traceable' mean for a measurement?

options.text: The measurement can be repeated
The instrument was calibrated against a reference standard, which itself was calibrated against a higher-tier standard, all the way back to the SI definition. Every step has a documented uncertainty
The instrument has a serial number
The measurement was published in a journal

items.reveal_title: Traceability chains and the redefined SI
items.reveal:
