In 2019 the SI was redefined so all seven base units are now derived from fundamental constants: the speed of light defines the metre, the Planck constant defines the kilogram (since 2019, replacing the platinum-iridium reference cylinder), the Boltzmann constant defines the kelvin, and so on.

A national metrology institute (NPL in the UK, NIST in the US) maintains primary realisations of these units. Industry calibration labs are calibrated against these primaries. Working labs send instruments to industry labs for periodic calibration.

When you read a balance display in a school lab, the number you see has a chain of calibration certificates behind it linking it back to the Planck constant via a Kibble balance.
items.why: Calibration is treated as paperwork. It is the substrate that makes any quantitative claim comparable across labs, countries and decades.

items.title: Reading a meniscus from the wrong angle changes the answer
items.claim: Read a burette with your eye above the meniscus: you see a high reading. Read with your eye below: a low reading. The error can be several percent — purely from where you put your head.
items.prompt: What's the right way to take the reading?

options.text: From wherever is comfortable
Eye level with the meniscus, viewing perpendicular to the scale, so the line of sight passes through the bottom of the meniscus and the scale at the same level
From slightly above to see the bottom of the meniscus better
From below to avoid disturbing the liquid

items.reveal:
Parallax error happens when the object you are reading and the scale you are reading against are at different distances from your eye. Any tilt in viewing angle shifts the apparent position of one relative to the other.

For a meniscus in a burette: the liquid surface and the scale on the burette tube are separated by a few millimetres. Looking down or up at an angle moves them apparently relative to each other.

Same problem with ammeters and voltmeters with mirror scales: align your eye so the needle and its reflection in the mirror coincide. This way you know you're looking perpendicular.

Digital readouts eliminate parallax (the reading is a single number). They introduce other concerns: rounding, response time, calibration drift.
items.why: Lab errors are taught as 'be careful'. Parallax is a specific systematic error with a specific fix — eye level, perpendicular sighting.

items.title: In space no one can hear you scream — sound needs a medium
items.claim: Sound is a pressure wave that propagates by compressing and rarefying particles of a medium. In a vacuum, there are no particles. Light travels through vacuum fine; sound cannot.
items.prompt: Why doesn't sound propagate in vacuum?

options.text: Vacuum is too cold
Sound is a mechanical wave — successive layers of atoms or molecules push on their neighbours. Without matter, there is no medium to compress and rarefy
Vacuum stops electromagnetic waves only
Sound requires gravity to propagate

items.reveal:
Sound is a longitudinal wave: layers of medium are compressed and rarefied in the direction of propagation. The wave needs a medium with mass (to carry inertia) and stiffness (to provide restoring force).

Electromagnetic waves (light, radio, X-rays) are different: they are self-supporting oscillations of electric and magnetic fields and need no medium. They cross interstellar vacuum easily.

Robert Boyle (1660) demonstrated this experimentally: he placed a ringing bell inside a glass jar and pumped out the air. As the air thinned, the bell sound faded. With a near-vacuum, no sound got out — but he could still see the clapper striking. The mechanical wave needed air; the light didn't.
items.why: Sound and light are both 'waves' — but require entirely different conditions to propagate. The vacuum distinguishes them sharply.

items.title: An ambulance's pitch drops as it passes you — and that drop is the Doppler effect
items.claim: An approaching ambulance siren sounds higher-pitched than its 'true' frequency; once it passes, the pitch suddenly drops. The shift is the Doppler effect, and it provides a quantitative way to measure radial velocity.
items.prompt: Why does the pitch change?

options.text: The siren plays different notes as it moves

Sound waves emitted by a source moving toward you are compressed (higher frequency, higher pitch); waves from a source moving away are stretched (lower frequency, lower pitch). The shift Δf/f equals v/c_sound
Your ears change sensitivity with movement
The siren only changes pitch in air

items.reveal:
For a source moving with speed v toward a stationary observer, the observed frequency is f_observed = f_source × c / (c - v), where c is the speed of sound. For source moving away, replace minus by plus.

At 30 m/s (a fast vehicle) and 343 m/s (speed of sound), the shift is about ±9 percent — easily heard as a pitch change of around a semitone.

The same effect applies to light. Astronomers measure stellar and galactic radial velocities by Doppler shifts of spectral lines. Most galaxies show redshifted spectra: they are moving away. This is how Hubble (1929) showed the universe is expanding.

Doppler weather radar bounces microwaves off raindrops and measures the frequency shift to find wind speeds at altitude. Police radar guns use the same principle to measure car speeds.
items.why: The Doppler effect is taught as 'pitch changes'. It is a universal feature of any wave and underlies tools from speed cameras to cosmology.

items.title: A bridge tore itself apart from a steady wind
items.claim: On 7 November 1940 the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington State collapsed after four months in service. A wind of about 19 m/s set the deck twisting at its torsional natural frequency. Within hours, the oscillation built up to several metres of amplitude and the structure failed.
items.prompt: How can a steady wind cause unbounded oscillation?

options.text: The wind happened to gust at exactly the right frequency
Aeroelastic flutter — the bridge's torsional motion changed the air flow in a way that fed energy back into the same motion at the same frequency, amplifying every cycle
The wind was much stronger than reported
The bridge was poorly maintained

items.reveal:
Driven resonance: a periodic external force at the natural frequency drives the oscillation higher each cycle. The amplitude grows linearly with time (limited by damping).

Aeroelastic flutter is different and more dangerous: the structure's own motion alters the airflow, which then drives the motion at the same frequency. It's a feedback loop where the driving frequency automatically locks to the response frequency. A steady wind suffices.

The Tacoma Narrows deck was an aerodynamically simple H-shape with a high aspect ratio. It was particularly vulnerable to torsional flutter at moderate wind speeds.

London's Millennium Bridge in 2000 had a similar story but with pedestrians instead of wind. Walkers' lateral footfalls synchronised with the bridge's natural side-to-side mode; the crowd unconsciously walked in step and amplified the swaying. The bridge was closed and dampers fitted.
items.why: Resonance is taught as benign (musical instruments). Aeroelastic flutter is its destructive cousin — and engineers must design against it explicitly.

items.title: Pitch, loudness and timbre are three independent properties of a sound
items.claim: A piano middle C and a flute middle C have the same pitch (frequency around 262 Hz). They sound completely different. A whisper and a shout at middle C have the same pitch but different loudness. Three independent dimensions describe a musical tone.
items.prompt: What's the physical basis of each?

options.text: All three are different combinations of frequency
Pitch corresponds to fundamental frequency; loudness corresponds to wave amplitude (intensity); timbre corresponds to the specific mixture of harmonics (overtones) above the fundamental
Pitch and loudness are the same physical quantity
Timbre is an illusion of the ear

items.reveal:
When a piano string vibrates at 262 Hz (middle C), it actually produces a complex waveform: a fundamental at 262 Hz plus harmonics at 524, 786, 1048 Hz etc. The relative strengths of those harmonics — and how they decay over time — give the piano its characteristic 'sound'.

A flute at the same note has very different harmonic content: stronger odd harmonics, less attack noise. A trumpet has yet another mix. The Fourier spectrum of a 'middle C' is a fingerprint of the instrument.

Loudness is approximately log of intensity. Decibel scale: 10 × log10(I/I0), where I0 is the threshold of hearing (about 10 to the minus 12 W/m²). A whisper is around 30 dB; conversational speech 60 dB; rock concert 120 dB. A 10 dB increase is about a doubling of perceived loudness.
items.why: Sound is often treated as 'a wave with a pitch'. It has three (and arguably more) independent properties that the ear perceives separately.

items.title: A guitar string vibrates at all its harmonics at once
items.claim: Pluck a guitar string. The note you hear has a fundamental frequency (say 110 Hz for an A2). But the string actually vibrates simultaneously in all the modes allowed by its end constraints: the fundamental, twice it (220 Hz), three times (330 Hz), and so on. The relative strengths of these harmonics give the guitar its sound.
items.prompt: Why these specific frequencies and no others?

options.text: The guitar maker tunes them

The string is fixed at both ends; allowed standing waves must have nodes at the endpoints, which restricts wavelengths to 2L/n where L is string length and n is an integer. Each n gives a different harmonic frequency
The string can only oscillate as a whole
The amplifier adds the harmonics electronically

items.reveal:
A string of length L fixed at both ends supports standing waves only if a whole number of half-wavelengths fits in the length: λ_n = 2L/n. The corresponding frequencies are f_n = n × v / (2L), where v is the wave speed along the string. The lowest mode (n=1) is the fundamental; n=2 is the first overtone (twice the fundamental); and so on.

The shape of a plucked string is the superposition of these allowed modes. The way you pluck (where and how) determines which modes get excited and with what amplitudes.

This is the simplest example of how boundary conditions select discrete energy levels in quantum mechanics. A particle confined to a box has discrete energies because its wavefunction must satisfy similar conditions at the box walls. Music and quantum mechanics are mathematically twins.
items.why: Strings are taught as 'they vibrate'. They vibrate in a specific spectrum dictated by their length and tension — and that spectrum is foundational to everything from music to spectroscopy.

items.title: A skydiver hits terminal velocity at around 55 m/s — and then doesn't get any faster
items.claim: Newton's second law says force equals mass times acceleration. A skydiver in free fall accelerates from gravity (about 9.8 m/s²) — but only briefly. Air resistance grows with speed until it balances gravity exactly. Then acceleration stops and the speed plateaus.
items.prompt: Why does air resistance grow with speed?

options.text: Air gets denser at higher speeds

Drag force scales as v squared (at high Reynolds numbers): the faster you move, the more air molecules you displace per second, and each is hit harder. At some speed, drag exactly cancels weight and net force is zero
Friction with the parachute slows you down
The Earth attracts faster objects more weakly

items.reveal:
For a falling body in air: net force = mg - (1/2)ρ C_d A v² (gravity minus drag, where ρ is air density, C_d the drag coefficient, A the frontal area, v the speed).

At terminal velocity v_t, net force is zero: v_t = √(2mg / ρ C_d A). For a belly-down skydiver: m about 80 kg, A about 0.7 m², C_d about 1.0 — gives v_t about 55 m/s (200 km/h).

In a head-down dive (smaller A, lower C_d), the same skydiver can reach 120 m/s or more. Felix Baumgartner reached 1357 km/h in his stratospheric jump (2012) — air density was very low at altitude so terminal velocity was much higher.

Deploying a parachute increases A by a factor of ~50, reducing v_t to a manageable 5-7 m/s for landing.
items.why: Newton's law for falling is taught as 'gravity gives constant acceleration'. Air drag bends the rule and gives a steady-state speed — which is what makes skydiving and parachuting work.

items.title: A pendulum trades potential and kinetic energy with no loss — in principle
items.claim: Pull a pendulum back to angle θ, release. At the bottom of the swing, all gravitational potential energy has become kinetic. Back at the top of the other side, all the kinetic energy is potential again. In an ideal frictionless pendulum, this swap continues forever.
items.prompt: Where does the energy actually go in a real pendulum?

options.text: It is destroyed at the bottom of the swing
Friction at the pivot, air resistance, and slight inelastic deformation of the string/rod all dissipate energy as heat. The amplitude decreases exponentially with each cycle (damped oscillation)
Energy is absorbed by Earth's gravitational field
Energy escapes as gravitational waves

items.reveal_title: Energy is conserved; the system simply transfers it out
items.reveal:
An ideal pendulum: m g L (1 - cos θ_max) of potential energy at the highest point becomes (1/2) m v² of kinetic energy at the bottom. The two trade places once per half-cycle.

A real pendulum loses some energy each cycle to friction at the pivot, drag through the air, and tiny inelastic effects in the string. The amplitude decays as exp(-t/τ) where τ is the time constant (typically minutes to hours for a good pendulum clock).

The pendulum's period for small angles is T = 2π√(L/g), independent of mass or amplitude. This is what made pendulum clocks accurate enough to be the global timekeeping standard from 1656 (Huygens) until ~1929 (when quartz oscillators overtook them).
items.why: Conservation of energy is taught as a static law. In a real oscillator it constrains where the energy goes — but it doesn't keep it all where you want it.

items.title: Centrifugal force is not a real force
items.claim: Swing a bucket on a string in a circle. People say a 'centrifugal force' pulls the water outward, keeping it pressed to the bucket. From an inertial frame outside the swing, no such force exists. The water's path is curved by the bucket pushing it INWARD.
items.prompt: What is actually keeping the water in the bucket?

options.text: An outward centrifugal force

Newton's first law — the water 'wants' to fly off in a straight line tangent to the circle. The bucket bottom provides a centripetal force inward that bends the water's path into a circle. From the bucket's rotating frame, that inward force appears as a fictitious outward 'centrifugal' force
Gravity holds the water down
Friction with the bucket sides

items.reveal_title: Centrifugal force is a frame artefact
items.reveal:
In an inertial (non-accelerating) reference frame, Newton's laws hold simply. Forces on the water: gravity (down) and normal force from bucket bottom (toward centre of circle). Net force is centripetal — bends the water's path.

In the bucket's rotating frame, the water appears stationary. To make Newton's laws apparently work in this non-inertial frame, you have to add fictitious forces: a centrifugal force pointing outward, equal in magnitude to the centripetal force. It explains the felt 'push' on the water against the bucket bottom.

Fictitious forces are mathematical conveniences. They are real-feeling because we live on a rotating planet — what we call 'down' includes a small centrifugal component that makes weighed objects slightly lighter at the equator than at the poles.

The Coriolis force is another fictitious force, also from rotation — and it shapes the rotation of cyclones, drift of ocean currents, and the long-range trajectories of artillery shells.
items.why: Centrifugal force is named like a real force. It's an accounting trick that appears only when you choose to do physics in a rotating frame.
